rebirth.intro: Does anything carry on after death, and if so, what? The Buddha said a stream of becoming continues without a fixed self. The Upanishads said the Self is untouched while the subtle body moves on. Plato told the Myth of Er. Theosophy and Steiner rebuilt the idea for the modern West. Start anywhere and keep going.

practices.name: The five remembrances
practices.how: Each day, recollect slowly: I am subject to ageing; to illness; to death; I will be parted from all that is dear; I am the owner of my actions, and will inherit them. Let each one sink in before the next.

practices.name: Mindfulness of death (maranasati)
practices.how: At nightfall and daybreak, reflect that death could come tonight or today from many causes, and ask whether any unskilful quality is still unabandoned. Let the urgency feed effort, not fear.

practices.name: Recollecting the round
practices.how: Contemplate how long the round of birth and death has been, and how many losses it holds, until disenchantment with becoming arises. Then turn to the breath and rest.

practices.name: Powa: an introduction to transference at death
practices.how: Read a traditional introduction before seeking instruction from a qualified teacher: refuge, visualising Amitabha above the crown, and training the mind's direction at death. It is taught with empowerment, not from a page.

practices.name: Preparing for the bardo
practices.how: Notice the small gaps of daily life (falling asleep, the pause between thoughts) as rehearsals for the great transition, and rest there as awareness.
practices.src: Lion's Roar: The Fine Art of Conscious Dying (Glenn Mullin)

practices.name: Self-enquiry: who dies?
practices.how: When the thought of death comes, ask to whom it comes. Trace the 'I' back to its source instead of following the thought. Ramana's own awakening began by lying down and enacting his death.
practices.src: Who Am I? (Sri Ramanasramam, free PDF)

practices.name: Practising dying (melete thanatou)
practices.how: Socrates calls philosophy the practice of dying: loosening the soul's grip on the body's pleasures and fears, day by day. Read the Phaedo slowly as an exercise, not an argument.

faith.intro: Devotion is the path of the heart: love turned toward the divine, a teacher, or a name. Bhakti sings it, Pure Land entrusts itself to Amida, the Sufi remembers God with every breath, the Christian prays without ceasing. Here the traditions describe what surrender is, and how it is practised.

reality.intro: Not two. Advaita says the world is Brahman appearing as many; Kashmir Shaivism says it is consciousness recognising itself; Dzogchen and Zen point to a nature that was never divided; the philosophers of the sacred ask whether mind comes first. Here is nonduality, and the question of what is real.

self/emptiness.intro: Form is emptiness, emptiness is form. For the Madhyamaka, nothing exists from its own side; for Zen, emptiness is this very moment; for Thich Nhat Hanh, it is interbeing; for Dzogchen, it is the open ground of mind. Here the Buddhist schools, and a few outside them, explain what emptiness is and is not.

imaginal.intro: Between the world of the senses and the world of pure ideas lies a third: the imaginal, Henry Corbin's word for the realm where visions, angels and archetypes are real. Sufis, Renaissance Platonists, Jung and Hillman, and today's scholars of myth and cosmology explore it. Here is imagination taken seriously.
